Given the significance of accurate prediction, this investigation undertakes a comparative analysis of the predictive capabilities of artificial neural network (ANN), standalone adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), and its hybrid counterpart integrated with particle swarm optimization (PSO). The focus lies on forecasting energy consumption in student residences based on climatic variables, with the University of Johannesburg's student housing serving as a specific case study. The input variables encompass ambient wind speed, wind direction, temperature, relative humidity, and atmospheric pressure, while the target variable is the corresponding energy consumption for student accommodation. Performance evaluation metrics such as root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), were employed to assess the efficacy of the developed models. Results obtained showed that the hybrid PSO-ANFIS outscored standalone ANN and ANFIS models with the lowest values of the RMSE, MAPE, and MAE, respectively. The developed model can aid in optimizing energy usage and support the design and dimensioning of alternative energy systems for campus housing.

articleTitle: Assessing Complementarity for Wind and Solar Energy in New Zealand
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Generation complementarity refers to the negative correlation between different types of generation, which effectively smoothens out intermittencies that have become prevalent with the increasing uptake of non-dispatchable generation such as wind turbine and solar PV generation. This paper presents the findings of temporal, spatial, and spatio-temporal complementarity studies conducted for New Zealand. The study utilizes 5 years’ worth of hourly observational data from local meteorological services and real power outputs of selected operating wind farms. The typical data pre-processing steps were applied after which Spearman’s Rank Correlation, Cross-correlation, and Canonical Correlation techniques were applied to the modelled power data and derived datasets to determine complementarity. Previous correlation studies published in New Zealand have not presented findings on wind-solar complementarity until recently. With the predicted uptake of these intermittent energy sources in multiple regions, this paper can provide a baseline for generation complementarity in New Zealand.

articleTitle: Vaffel - a tool for forecasting transmission line failures based on Bayesian updating, renalysis data and medium range weather forecasts
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: This paper presents a method for forecasting the probability of weather-related transmission line failures. The method combines failure statistics, a Bayesian updating scheme and reanalysis weather data to produce fragility curves that model the relationship between weather exposure for a component and the probability of failure. The fragility curves are combined with medium range weather forecasts extracted at each span of the individual transmission lines to obtain a forecast of the hourly probability of failure for each line. A tool that implements the method has been developed and is currently being tested operationally within the Norwegian TSO Statnett. We show the data requirements and demonstrate the use of a dashboard that expose the forecasts to an end-user.

articleTitle: Time-Dependent Transmission Capacity Model for Long-Term Operating Reserve Assessment
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Transmission network capacity needs to be regularly reinforced either by building new transmission lines or upgrading existing circuits. Moreover, expansion planning processes always consider deterministic static thermal ratings as the basis of the N-1 security criterion to meet the growing electricity demands. This paper proposes a probabilistic framework to assess the inclusion of a time-dependent transmission capacity model in expansion planning studies, enabled by dynamic line rating (DLR) technology application. This work first exploits the multivariate requirements associated with DLR-based approaches, discussing the use of electrical, mechanical and thermal variables. Next, a probabilistic framework is built to demonstrate the effectiveness of DLR technology by assessing reliability indices through a sequential Monte Carlo simulation. To illustrate the proposed approach, the IEEE-RTS GMLC 2019 and high voltage transmission line data of the Brazilian interconnected system are utilized. Numerical results show that the proposed approach can be used to certify the inclusion of DLR-based technology in the list of possible alternatives to reinforce transmission systems.

articleTitle: Mitigating the Impact of Uncertain Wildfire Risk on Power Grids through Topology Control
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Wildfires pose a significant threat to the safe and reliable operations of the electric grid. To mitigate wildfire risk, system operators resort to public safety power shutoffs, or PSPS, that shed load for a subset of customers. As wildfire risk forecasts are stochastic, such decision-making may often be sub-optimal. This paper proposes a two-stage topology control problem that jointly minimizes generation and load-shedding costs in the face of uncertain fire risk. Compared to existing work, we include pre-and post-event topology control actions and consider scenarios where the wildfire risk is known with low and high confidence. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated using a benchmark test system, artificially geo-located in Southern California, and using stochastic wildfire risk data that exists in the literature. Our work provides a crucial study of the comparative benefits of pre-event versus post-event control and the effects of wildfire risk accuracy on each control strategy.

articleTitle: Probabilistic Forecasting of High-Frequency Voltage Distortions in Low-Voltage Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Waveform distortion disturbances deteriorate Power Quality (PQ) in power systems and affect electrical installations and equipment. In modern Low-Voltage (LV) distribution systems, electrical signals are characterized by the contemporaneous presence of low-frequency and High-Frequency (HF) spectral components (i.e., up to 150 kHz). This paper focuses on HF voltage distortions, also known as supraharmonics, that can create losses and reduce the efficiency of the equipment. Accurate predictions of future HF voltage distortions help distribution system operators and regulators in taking timely actions to define and withstand PQ limits or to analyze the residual capacity of networks toward the additional installation of power electronic converters. This paper provides a probabilistic approach to forecast HF voltage distortions by applying a methodology based on Quantile Regression Forests (QRFs). Results of numerical experiments based on publicly available actual data collected at a LV distribution system are presented to assess the performance of the proposed methodology.

articleTitle: Sample Size Selection for Monte Carlo Resource Adequacy Assessment of Power Systems
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Choosing the number of Monte Carlo samples to use in a probabilistic resource adequacy assessment requires striking a balance between computational expense and the statistical precision of study results. This paper reviews the conventional Central Limit Theorem approach to quantifying result confidence in Monte Carlo analysis, and then introduces two new methods that address shortcomings in this approach when applied in the context of resource adequacy assessment.The first alternative provides a lower bound on adequacy confidence in the case of all-zero sample observations, a common occurrence in resource adequacy analysis that the Central Limit Theorem method is ill-equipped to handle. The second alternative uses Bayesian conjugate priors to learn from outcome samples more efficiently, reducing sample size requirements if an appropriate prior distribution can be provided. Both of these methods’ potential advantages over the traditional approach are demonstrated via empirical comparisons of sample size requirements and inference error in resource adequacy assessment of a test system.

articleTitle: Enhancing Grid Security through Bilevel Optimization of Aggregated Distributed Energy Resources for Flexible Operation in Distribution Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: This paper proposes a bilevel optimization strategy addressing the impact of aggregated distributed energy resources (DER) on distribution networks to ensure grid security. The first optimization level is the network reconfiguration model, which addresses a gap where existing models prioritize economic objectives over security constraints. The model incorporates probabilistic scenarios and proposes a probabilistic voltage risk index and hosting capacity to minimize total distribution network power loss. The second optimization level is the flexibility estimation process, which applies a decision tree classification algorithm to determine the minimum flexibility (MW) for the desired voltage deviation reduction. Where existing models are only suitable for offline estimation, the proposed approach is suitable for online flexibility estimation. Tested on the IEEE 33 network, the proposed technique yields a 16.67% improvement in worst-node voltage deviation under a 100% load increase. The results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed bilevel technique in optimizing network configuration and estimating flexibility support, ultimately enhancing the collaboration between transmission and distribution network operators.

articleTitle: Assigning Capacity Credit to Demand Response
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Renewable energy sources (RES) are assuming an increasing role in mitigating global gas emissions by replacing conventional generation. However, the output power of dominant sources, photovoltaic (PV) and wind turbine (WT) are intermittent since they depend on uncertain factors, i.e., solar irradiation and wind speed. To address the variability, this study employs a battery energy storage system (BESS) to help balance supply and demand. If the BESS is insufficient, demand response (DR) is considered as a virtual power plant (VPP) to reduce the risk of load loss. Additionally, multi-objective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) is used to enhance the reliability and cost-efficiency of integrated renewable energy sources (RESs) such as photovoltaic (PV), wind turbines (WT), BESS, and DR. The research investigates stand-alone systems both with and without DR, finding the optimal solution through fuzzy logic. System planning is based on the combined system’s size, with capacity credit (CC) analysis of the optimal solution achieved via genetic algorithm optimization (GA). The CC is estimated using the effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) method. Various reliability indices, including daily loss of load expectation (LOLE), hourly loss of load (LOLH), and expected energy not served (EENS), are applied to assess their impact on CC.

articleTitle: Energy Management System for Residential Electric Vehicles: A New Zealand based Case Study
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Electric Vehicles (EVs) offer a sustainable transportation option. As EV adoption grows, there will be a significant increase in demand for residential distribution networks that include charging infrastructure. As a result, significant advancements have been made in this field of research in recent years. This paper proposes a comprehensive Energy Management System (EMS) for a residential area equipped with an EV charging system. The developed EMS consists of two components: forecasting EV charging demand (Monte Carlo Simulation), residential load demand (OLS Regression), electricity prices (LSTM), and optimizing EV charge scheduling. The results show that the developed EMS is able to reduce the system cost significantly while also reducing peak network demand. The analysis of uncertainty indicates that cost savings range between 4.1% and 11.8%, with an average of 7.4%. The case studies highlight the economic advantages of the suggested approach.

articleTitle: Analysis of Historical Power Outages of the United States and the National Risk Index
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: Several works have been documented in the literature to study the societal effect of power outages and to analyze their correlation with the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI). However, the relationship between National Risk Index (NRI) and power outages is yet to be explored. This work analyzes the NRI indices such as Risk, Expected Annual Loss, Social Vulnerability, and Community Resilience with several resilience metrics such as event duration, impact duration, recovery duration, impact level, impact rate, recovery rate, recovery to impact ratio, and area under the outage curves to see the correlation of NRI indices with the resilience metrics. The results show that NRI indices such as Risk and Expected Annual Loss increase with the increase of event duration, impact duration, and recovery duration. All Other metrics are indifferent to the change in the Risk and EAL ratings. The results also show that there is no strong relationship between all the metrics and community resilience and social vulnerability. This work also performed the sensitivity analysis of the extreme event selection process. This sensitivity analysis reveals that the way of identifying extreme events has a significant impact on the evaluation of the events.

articleTitle: Transmission Planning Perspectives for the New Uncertainties in Power Systems
publicationTitle: 2024 18th International Conference on Probabilistic Methods Applied to Power Systems (PMAPS)
abstract: The long-term studies of power systems involving generation and transmission infrastructure usually consider the estimation of indices to identify, for instance, possible bottlenecks within electrical or energetic assets. Current planning concerns such as the reduction of inertia in hybrid interconnected power systems, the need for flexibility of generation and transmission systems to cope with rapid variations linked to wind and solar generation, the inherent degradation in power quality connected with the massive use of power electronic devices connected to the grid, are demanding a revision of the traditional planning process of power systems. This paper presents a set of probabilistic planning studies addressing the changes in the generation systems, mainly replacing synchronous generating units, namely thermal machines, for asynchronous generating units, such as wind turbines. The main purpose of these planning perspectives is to verify the impact of these changes on the transmission system and the operating system risk. The simulation is based on the IEEE RTS GMLC 2019.
